analysis.one_liner: Raises penalties for monopolies and makes it easier for enforcers to block large mergers.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 11 Democratic cosponsors in May 2024, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the nation's antitrust laws to make it easier for the Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission to stop big corporate mergers and punish dominant companies that squeeze out competitors. It would let regulators impose fines of up to 15 percent of a company's U.S. revenue for monopolization, lower the bar for blocking mergers over $5 billion, protect and reward whistleblowers who report price-fixing, and stop companies from forcing antitrust disputes into arbitration. It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, consumers, and small businesses. The bill targets monopsony power — big employers who hold wages down by limiting workers' options — and dominant firms whose conduct raises prices or shuts out smaller rivals. It would also help private plaintiffs recover triple damages with interest and end forced arbitration for antitrust class actions, and would pay whistleblowers 10 to 30 percent of criminal fines their tips produce.

how_it_helps.text: The bill changes the merger standard from showing a merger would 'substantially to lessen' competition to showing it creates an 'appreciable risk of materially lessening' competition, and shifts the burden of proof onto the merging companies for very large deals — those over $5 billion, or involving firms over $100 billion buying targets over $50 million [S2].

It explicitly covers monopsony power — when a dominant buyer or employer forces suppliers to take below-market prices or workers to accept below-market wages — and lets enforcers treat mergers that create a monopsony as illegal [S2].

It creates civil penalties of up to the greater of 15 percent of a company's total U.S. revenue or 30 percent of its revenue in the affected line of commerce for Sherman Act violations and exclusionary conduct by firms with more than 50 percent market share [S2].
It bars companies from enforcing pre-dispute arbitration agreements or class-action waivers in antitrust cases, allowing consumers and businesses to sue as a class in court [S2].

It protects employees, contractors, and agents from retaliation for reporting antitrust violations and lets them recover back pay and damages, plus rewards of 10 to 30 percent of criminal fines for information leading to enforcement [S2].

It authorizes $535 million for the Justice Department's Antitrust Division and $725 million for the FTC for fiscal 2025, funded in later years by merger filing fees, and creates new FTC offices to track market concentration and merger outcomes [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large dominant corporations and frequent merger-makers would pay, through fines, tougher merger reviews, and post-merger reporting certified by executives under penalty of perjury. Some costs could be passed to consumers through prices, and taxpayers fund the higher agency budgets in the first year.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large dominant corporations and merger parties

drawbacks.text: Companies seeking to merge over $5 billion would bear the burden of proving their deal won't harm competition, which could deter or slow mergers that would actually create efficiencies or help the merging firms compete with larger rivals [S2].

Conduct by any firm with more than 50 percent market share would be presumed to violate the law unless the firm proves procompetitive benefits — a broad standard that could expose ordinary business practices, including some pricing and platform conduct, to litigation and penalties even without proven consumer harm [S2].

Fines calculated as a share of total company revenue — up to 15 percent of all U.S. revenue — could reach into the tens of billions for the largest firms, and some portion of those costs would likely be passed through to consumers; the first-year agency funding increase would also fall on taxpayers until merger fees take over [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would meaningfully shift power toward regulators, workers, and smaller competitors in markets where a handful of firms dominate, and its whistleblower and anti-arbitration provisions would strengthen private enforcement. The trade-offs are real: the low legal bar ('appreciable risk') and revenue-based penalties could deter some beneficial deals and business conduct, and errors would fall on companies and their customers as well as on the dominant firms targeted. Whether the deterrence benefits outweigh over-enforcement depends on how aggressively future administrations apply it, since the bill leaves penalty amounts largely to agency discretion under guidelines.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the two-year Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar and 11 Democratic cosponsors introduced the Competition and Antitrust Law Enforcement Reform Act of 2024 on May 9, 2024 [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; no further action appears in the record [S2][S4].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, floor vote, or House action is recorded before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large companies that dominate their markets are better off: they face no higher merger scrutiny, no revenue-based penalties, and no new exposure to antitrust class actions or whistleblower reports. Workers, consumers, and small businesses gain nothing from the bill's death, but lose the protections it would have provided.

for.name: Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 11 Democratic cosponsors; her antitrust enforcement reform proposal

for.name: Blumenthal, Whitehouse, Hirono, Booker, Welch, Warner, Wyden, Heinrich, Markey, Schatz, and Smith
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, all as Democrats

against.name: Dick Durbin
against.what_they_did: The committee never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the two-year Congress, leaving it without a vote

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator cosponsored the bill, and it received no floor consideration

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never reached the floor, so support was entirely one-party.

industries.industry: Large dominant corporations (big tech, pharmaceutical, healthcare, and platform firms)
industries.note: Firms with over 50 percent market share would face a presumption of liability for exclusionary conduct and civil penalties up to 15 percent of total U.S. revenue. These firms profit from market positions the bill targets, at a cost to the consumers and workers they charge or underpay.

industries.industry: Serial acquirers and merger-and-acquisition-driven firms (including large private equity and institutional buyers)
industries.note: Deals over $5 billion — or by $100 billion firms buying targets over $50 million — would be presumed anticompetitive unless the acquirer proves otherwise, with mandatory 5-year post-merger reporting certified by executives. A decade saw over $10 trillion in U.S. mergers and acquisitions, so the bill directly limits this business model.

industries.industry: Antitrust defense bar and corporate legal departments
industries.note: Tougher enforcement, new penalties, and mandatory reporting would increase demand for antitrust defense work, raising legal costs for corporations that would likely be passed through to customers.
